title: The Parish of Little Hawley
premise: Juniper Crane has spent years listening to Little Hawley through a radio headset, solving deaths the police misfiled as accidents while remaining a ghost herself. When a confession letter for the drowning of her own mother arrives postmarked the day after the funeral, Juniper realizes someone in her small town knew the truth all along—and knew her well enough to torment her with it. Following the letter's clues through tide charts, church records, and the taxi company's oldest ledgers, she uncovers a cover-up woven through the parish's most respected families, including her estranged father's. In the end, Juniper must choose between exposing the killer and protecting the one person left who loves her, and she discovers that belonging means being seen, even when it costs everything.
about_author: J. M. Delacroix is the pen name of a former emergency dispatcher who spent eleven years on the night shift in a coastal town much like Little Hawley, listening to the dark so others could sleep. They now write mysteries about quiet people who notice everything.

chapters.title: The Frequency of Small Towns
chapters.summary: Juniper Crane works the night shift at Little Hawley Taxi, mapping the town through the voices that call her. POV Juniper. Establishes her invisibility, her habit of noticing what others miss, and the three 'accidents' she quietly unraveled. Emotional beat: lonely competence—the comfort of being unheard but never blind.

chapters.title: What the Tide Kept
chapters.summary: Twenty years after her mother drowned, Juniper attends the funeral of Edith Marsh, the woman who pulled her mother from the water too late. POV Juniper. At the graveside she notices Edith's daughter watching her with something like guilt. Emotional beat: grief resurfacing in a town that treats the past as settled.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: A letter arrives confessing to the drowning of Juniper's mother—postmarked the day after Edith's funeral. POV Juniper. The handwriting is careful, anonymous, and knows details never made public. Emotional beat: the floor drops out of her carefully ordered life; invisibility was never a shield.

chapters.title: Three Accidents and a Lie
chapters.summary: Juniper reviews her old case files—the three deaths police called accidents—and finds Edith Marsh connected to all three as a witness. POV Juniper. Emotional beat: cold dread hardening into method; the letter isn't a confession, it's a summons.

chapters.title: The Dispatcher's Ear
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter to Juniper's first solved death, told through her memory of a single panicked phone call. POV Juniper. Shows how she taught herself forensics from radio chatter and library books. Emotional beat: origin story—why she can't let the letter go unanswered.

chapters.title: Father Calloway's Ledger
chapters.summary: Juniper consults the parish records and finds Edith Marsh had been quietly paying the church for twenty years—amounts matching hush money. POV Juniper and a brief interlude from Father Calloway, who burns a page. Emotional beat: the parish itself is complicit; sanctity and rot share a roof.

chapters.title: The Man Who Drives the Night Route
chapters.summary: Juniper's closest friend, taxi driver Sam Okafor, admits he's been driving a mysterious weekly passenger to the cliffs for years—paid in cash by Edith Marsh. POV Sam. Emotional beat: loyalty tested; Sam realizes his kindness was used as a blindfold.

chapters.title: Salt and Silence
chapters.summary: Juniper walks the cliff path where her mother died, reconstructing the tide that night using old weather logs. POV Juniper. The drowning couldn't have happened where the police said. Emotional beat: the first hard proof; her mother's death was staged, and the town helped bury it.

chapters.title: The Crane House
chapters.summary: Juniper confronts her estranged father, Aldous, a retired harbor master, who refuses to discuss the letter but flinches at her mother's name. POV Aldous. Emotional beat: love against duty—Aldous knows something and chose his reputation over his daughter, and knows it.

chapters.title: Someone Is Following the Cab
chapters.summary: Juniper notices the same car trailing Sam's night route; the letter writer is watching her investigation. POV Juniper. She baits the follower with a false lead. Emotional beat: hunter becomes hunted; fear sharpens into defiance.

chapters.title: Edith's Daughter
chapters.summary: Juniper finally speaks with Ruth Marsh, who confesses her mother received anonymous payments for decades to keep silent about 'the Crane woman.' POV Ruth. Emotional beat: two daughters of secrets recognizing each other; Ruth is terrified, not guilty.

chapters.title: The Passenger to the Cliffs
chapters.summary: Sam identifies the weekly passenger from an old dispatch log: it was the town's beloved doctor, Gerald Vane, now dying in a care home. POV Sam. Emotional beat: the horror of realizing the town's kindest face may be its darkest.

chapters.title: What Dying Men Confess
chapters.summary: Juniper visits Dr. Vane, who is too far gone to speak clearly but writes one word: 'Aldous.' POV Juniper. Emotional beat: the letter's author may be Vane—or Vane may be another victim of the truth.

chapters.title: The Second Letter
chapters.summary: A second letter arrives, threatening Sam by name if Juniper keeps digging. POV Juniper. She realizes the writer has access to dispatch logs—someone inside the taxi company. Emotional beat: paranoia closes in; nowhere in Little Hawley is neutral ground.

chapters.title: The Night Manager
chapters.summary: Juniper investigates her own office and finds the company's owner, Margaret Fenn, altered dispatch records the week of the drowning. POV Margaret. Emotional beat: the banality of complicity—Margaret was paid to lose one page and has carried it for twenty years.

chapters.title: Aldous Breaks
chapters.summary: Juniper corners her father with the tide evidence; Aldous admits he saw Vane with her mother that night and was paid to falsify the harbor log. POV Aldous. Emotional beat: love against duty collapses—his confession destroys the last family Juniper had.

chapters.title: The Tide Gives Up What It Took
chapters.summary: A storm uncovers her mother's belongings on the shore, including a locket holding a photo of Vane and a date. POV Juniper. Her mother and Vane had a secret relationship; the drowning was no accident of passion but a silencing. Emotional beat: her mother becomes a person, not a mystery.

chapters.title: Who Wrote the Confession
chapters.summary: Juniper traces the letter's paper to the care home's stationery—Vane wrote the confession before dying, mailed posthumously by Ruth's mother's instruction, to force the truth out. POV Ruth. Emotional beat: the confession was a dying man's gift and a trap sprung too well.

chapters.title: The Last Passenger
chapters.summary: Juniper and Sam stake out the cliff road; the follower appears—Margaret Fenn's brother, the constable who closed the drowning case, sent to retrieve Vane's letters. POV alternating Juniper and the constable. Emotional beat: the machinery of the cover-up exposed, desperate and cornered.

chapters.title: Cliffside
chapters.summary: Climax: the constable, panicked, forces Juniper toward the cliff edge where her mother died; Sam and Ruth arrive, and Juniper—using her dispatcher's calm—talks him down while recording his confession. POV Juniper. Emotional beat: the invisible woman makes the whole town listen at last.

chapters.title: What the Parish Owes
chapters.summary: The cover-up unravels publicly: Margaret, Aldous, and the constable face consequences; the parish's complicity becomes the town's reckoning. POV multiple brief voices. Emotional beat: justice is messy and insufficient, but the silence is broken.

chapters.title: Juniper Crane, By Name
chapters.summary: Months later, Juniper takes a job consulting for the police, introduced at a town meeting by her full name. She visits her mother's restored grave with Sam beside her. POV Juniper. Emotional beat: resolution—belonging was never given to her; she claimed it, and the town finally sees her.
